analysis.one_liner: Forces approval of the Keystone XL pipeline and strips environmental review within 30 days.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in four House committees for the rest of the 113th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the Secretary of State to approve TransCanada's Keystone XL pipeline permit within 30 days and to declare the finished environmental review, without further study. It would have cut the pay of senior State, Interior, and Army officials by up to 25% if they did not comply, and ordered the Interior and Army departments to issue all remaining pipeline permits on the same deadline. It was referred to four committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: TransCanada and the oil industry, which would get a guaranteed cross-border pipeline permit without completing the normal federal environmental review, plus refiners and shippers of Canadian oil sands crude.

how_it_helps.text: Orders the Secretary of State to issue the Presidential permit for Keystone XL within 30 days of enactment, based on TransCanada's 2012 application as updated for the Nebraska reroute [S2] [S3].

Declares that the final environmental impact statement plus Nebraska's state review satisfy all requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Endangered Species Act, cutting off further federal environmental review [S2] [S3].
Orders the Interior and Army secretaries to issue every remaining pipeline permit — including right-of-way across federal land and Clean Water Act wetland permits — within 30 days [S2] [S3].

Enforces the deadlines by barring federal funds from paying more than 75% of the salaries of the Secretary of State, senior State officials, the Interior Secretary, and Army civil-works officials until the permits are issued [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had passed, the costs would fall on communities along the pipeline route and on federal agencies stripped of their review authority; the country would have foregone the completed review that normally informs a cross-border permit decision, and critics warned of spills over the Ogallala aquifer and of locking in additional carbon-intensive oil sands crude.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities along the route and agencies' review authority

drawbacks.text: The bill replaces the ordinary environmental review process with a legislatively mandated conclusion — a state report plus a federal draft review would be deemed to satisfy three major environmental statutes, so no agency could revisit the findings [S3].

The 75% salary penalty attempts to pressure named executive officials into issuing a permit by a fixed date, which the Obama administration opposed; the President's own review was still under way, and this would have ended it by statute rather than evidence.

Approving the pipeline would enable increased transport of Canadian oil sands crude, whose extraction and refining are more carbon-intensive than conventional oil — a cost borne globally rather than by the bill's beneficiaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated and immediate: a guaranteed permit and a construction timeline for one company and its customers in the oil industry. The costs — weakened environmental review, a precedent for Congress to override agency findings on major projects, and the carbon impact of oil sands crude — are diffuse and long-term. For ordinary people the trade is poor.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in December 2013 and referred to four House committees, it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 11, 2013 with no cosponsors [S4] and referred the same day to four committees: Transportation and Infrastructure, Foreign Affairs, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources [S5].
By December 17 it had been sent to four subcommittees (Railroads, Pipelines and Hazardous Materials; Energy and Power; Energy and Mineral Resources; Public Lands and Environmental Regulation) [S5].
No further action is recorded; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one, strictly — the bill simply went nowhere. Had it moved, its beneficiaries would have been TransCanada and oil sands shippers; its death left the existing environmental review process and the administration's timeline in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill died in committee

for.name: Jack Kingston
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 11, 2013 and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the four committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the 113th Congress.

against.name: Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: The administration was conducting its own Keystone XL review and opposed congressional deadlines forcing a permit decision before it concluded.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of any potential floor fight is unknown from the record.

industries.note: The bill's entire purpose is to hand TransCanada a guaranteed federal permit within 30 days, bypassing the remaining federal environmental review. The gain to the company would come at the cost of weakened review authority for affected communities.
Keystone XL is the main export route for growing oil sands production; a legislatively guaranteed permit would improve market access regardless of the outcome of the standard review.

The bill would nullify the agencies' statutory role in reviewing the project and would penalize their senior officials' pay for noncompliance — a direct cut to institutional authority, not a benefit to the officials themselves.
